analysis.one_liner: Applies state consumer-protection laws, including anti-predatory-lending rules, to national banks and federal thrifts.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee vote and died in the House Financial Services Committee when the 110th Congress ended in January 2009.
analysis.plain_summary: At the time, national banks and federal savings associations were largely shielded by their federal regulators from state consumer laws. This bill would have applied state consumer-protection laws — including rules against unfair and deceptive practices, consumer fraud, and predatory high-cost mortgage lending — directly to national banks and federal thrifts [S2] [S3]. It also would have let state attorneys general sue those banks on behalf of residents, limited regulators' power to preempt state law, required the regulators to log and publicly report consumer complaints, and confirmed that state law still applies to nonbank subsidiaries and agents of national banks [S3].
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers who borrow from or bank with national banks and federal savings associations — especially mortgage borrowers in states with strong anti-predatory-lending laws — would gain the same legal protections that state-chartered lenders already face. State attorneys general would gain clear authority to sue national banks and federal thrifts on behalf of their residents and recover damages for them, and private customers would retain the right to enforce their rights in court even when a federal regulator brings its own enforcement action [S3]. The public would also get semi-annual, publicly posted reports on how many complaints the regulators received and how they resolved them [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Bank customers and state attorneys general

how_it_helps.text: Declares that state consumer laws of general application — covering unfair or deceptive acts, consumer fraud, repossession, foreclosure, and collection — apply to national banks and federal savings associations, ending their exemption from those state rules [S2] [S3].

Applies state laws providing greater protection against high-cost predatory mortgage loans than federal Truth in Lending rules, so national banks and thrifts must follow the toughest state anti-predatory-lending standards [S2] [S3].

Explicitly protects the authority of state attorneys general to sue national banks and federal savings associations to enforce federal or state law and to recover damages for state residents, and confirms that private parties can still enforce their rights in court [S3].

Requires the Comptroller of the Currency and the Office of Thrift Supervision to record every consumer complaint, document how it was resolved, and publish semi-annual reports to Congress and on their websites [S2] [S3].

Bars federal preemption of state law for state-chartered nondepository subsidiaries and agents of national banks and thrifts — closing the 'rent-a-bank' route some lenders used to escape state rules through a bank charter [S3].
Provides that a loan not entitled to preemption when made keeps that status even if later acquired by a national bank, preventing banks from buying their way out of state-law liability [S3].

analysis.who_pays: National banks and federal savings associations would bear the cost: they would have to comply with up to 50 state consumer-protection regimes, follow stricter state anti-predatory-lending rules, and face lawsuits from state attorneys general and private litigants that their federal regulators currently shield them from. The Comptroller and the Office of Thrift Supervision would also lose much of their discretion to preempt state law, since they could do so only where a comparable federal statute expressly governs the activity [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: National banks and federal savings associations

drawbacks.text: The bill sharply restricts when the Comptroller and the thrift regulator may preempt state law, allowing it only where a comparable federal statute expressly governs the activity — a stricter standard than the preemption rules in force at the time, and one banks argued made it hard to operate under a single national rulebook [S3].

Making up to 50 sets of state consumer laws apply to nationally chartered banks would raise compliance costs, and banks contended that patchwork state rules could ultimately be passed on to customers through higher fees — the classic trade-off between uniform national standards and stronger local protections [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would have given bank and mortgage customers the same state-law protections that state-chartered lenders already faced, at a moment when national banks were exempt from many state anti-predatory-lending laws while making the riskiest loans of the era. The cost is real but the trade-off it strikes is a familiar one: banks lose the convenience of one national rulebook, while consumers gain stronger remedies and a state enforcement backstop. On balance the consumer protections outweigh the compliance burden, though the bill does little to harmonize state rules with each other.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Financial Services Committee and then to a subcommittee, and neither ever held a markup or vote, so it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Luis Gutierrez introduced the bill on April 23, 2007, joined by Reps. Ron Paul, Julia Carson, Wm. Lacy Clay, and Sheila Jackson Lee as original cosponsors [S3].
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services the same day it was introduced [S1] [S5].
On June 7, 2007, it was referred to the subcommittee on Financial Institutions and Consumer Credit — the last action ever taken on it [S5].
No hearing, markup, or floor vote ever occurred, and the bill expired when the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: National banks and federal savings associations came out ahead: they kept the federal-preemption shield that exempted them from state consumer-protection laws and state attorneys general lawsuits through the rest of the decade.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was sponsored by a Democrat but counted a Republican, Rep. Ron Paul, among its four cosponsors, and its only obstacles were procedural inaction rather than an opposing vote.

industries.note: The bill strips national banks of the federal-preemption shield their regulator used to exempt them from state consumer-protection and anti-predatory-lending laws, and exposes them to state attorney general suits and private litigation. Their interest in keeping preemption ran directly against customers seeking state-law remedies.

Same treatment as national banks: state consumer laws, state predatory-lending rules, and state enforcement would apply to thrifts regulated by the Office of Thrift Supervision, which currently could preempt those state laws.

industries.industry: Nonbank subsidiaries and agents of national banks and thrifts
industries.note: The bill confirms state law applies to state-chartered nondepository subsidiaries and agents of banks, closing a channel some consumer lenders used to escape state rules by affiliating with a bank.
